world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Krinkova, Zuzana 2015. From Iberian Romani to Iberian Para-Romani varieties (Karolinum); Glottolog refs otherwise wordlists/sociolinguistics - full text not reached

new_statements.quote: V naší práci se v případě iberských (para)romštin přidržujeme, co se zápisu přízvuku týče, vždy konkrétního pramene. Je však nutné upozornit na fakt, že starší prameny (ke caló) přízvuky někdy zcela opomíjejí. [...] problematiku přízvuku v iberských pararomštinách ponecháváme na případnou budoucí studii. K tomuto tématu lze prozatím obecně konstatovat, že pravděpodobný raně romský přízvuk je v iberských (para)romštinách poměrně dobře doložen, což dokládají např. četná adjektiva v caló končící přízvučnou samohláskou.
new_statements.translation: In our work, for the Iberian (Para-)Romani varieties we always follow the particular source as regards the marking of stress. It must be pointed out, however, that the older sources (on Caló) sometimes omit stress marks entirely. [...] we leave the question of stress in the Iberian Para-Romani varieties to a possible future study. On this topic it can for now be stated in general that the probable Early Romani stress is fairly well attested in the Iberian (Para-)Romani varieties, as shown e.g. by the numerous adjectives in Caló ending in a stressed vowel.
new_statements.citation: Krinková, Zuzana. 2013. Vzájemné ovlivňování romštiny, španělštiny a dalších jazyků Pyrenejského poloostrova. PhD dissertation, Univerzita Karlova v Praze, Filozofická fakulta.
new_statements.locator: printed p. 69 (PDF p. 73), end of sect. 3.2 'Několik poznámek k pravopisu a fonetické transkripci', immediately before 3.2.1. (The PDF text layer renders 'á' as a bar glyph; diacritics restored in the quote.)
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: (318 pp., Word 2010, author metadata 'Zuzana Krinková'), PDF p. 73 = printed p. 69, last paragraph of sect. 3.2 before the heading '3.2.1 Ortografické zvláštnosti španělského caló'. The passage is there word for word; the only differences are (a) the PDF text layer renders 'á' as a bar glyph ('pr|ci', 'samohl|skou'), which the first reader restored, and (b) the first reader's '[...]' elides two sentences ('U výchozích romských tvarů zpravidla označujeme přízvuky... V tomto ohledu jsme si vědomi určité nejednotnosti, kterou snad lze částečně omluvit tím, že') without changing the sense. Translation is accurate. The other locators cited also check out in the saved 265 on p. 158 '…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No source gives a positional stress rule for Caló as a whole. Caló is a mixed language whose phonology and inflection are (Andalusian) Spanish, so stress placement is lexical/Spanish-type; within the Romani-derived lexical stock the Early Romani word-final stress is largely retained (oxytone nouns and adjectives in -ó, -í, -é, -á, -ú: baró, chororí, gachó), while Spanish-derived words and Spanish inflections keep their Spanish stress (Quindalé 1870: Castilian-origin adjectives in unstressed -o/-e 'siguen las mismas reglas de su origen').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: Krinková notes stress shifts in individual suffixes: -unó > -úno in later loan integration (fn. 265, p. 158) and comparative -edér > productive -eta with stress shift (p. 158); older Caló sources often omit accent marks, so stress of many recorded forms is unrecoverable. Quindalé 1870 (pp. 51, 64-65) contrasts inherited words ending in a consonant or stressed vowel with Castilian-derived words ending in unstressed -o/-e.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns the etymological (Romani-derived) lexicon in citation forms as recorded in 17th-21st c. written sources, not a synchronic prosodic analysis; Krinková explicitly defers a study of stress. Quindalé 1870 p. 49 states Caló has 'la misma escritura, alfabeto, ortografía y demás estructura gramatical que el castellano'.
new_statements.identity_note: Both quoted sources treat 'caló' = the Spanish (chiefly Andalusian-based) Para-Romani of the Gitanos, i.e. Glottolog calo1236 / ISO rmq; Krinková's remark is phrased for the Iberian (Para-)Romani varieties as a group (Spanish caló plus Catalan and Basque Para-Romani, the latter = Erromintxela emx, erro1240) but the evidence cited is Caló adjectives. Quindalé 1870 describes 19th-century Spanish Caló (Madrid/Andalusia). Caló is a mixed language: grammar and phonology Spanish, lexicon partly Romani, so any 'stress rule' is that of the Spanish frame with an oxytone Romani-derived stratum.

sources.note: p. 69 (sect. 3.2): stress marking follows each source; older Caló sources often omit accents; the question of stress in Iberian Para-Romani is left to a future study, but 'the probable Early Romani stress is fairly well attested in Iberian (Para-)Romani, as shown e.g. by the numerous Caló adjectives ending in a stressed vowel'. Elsewhere only stress shifts in individual suffixes (-unó > -úno, -edér > -eta) and that Caló is fully adapted to the Spanish phonological system (p. 226). No other stress rule stated (grep of full text for přízvuk/přízvučn-/slabik-).

sources.citation: Quindalé, Francisco [= Francisco de Sales Mayo]. 1870. El gitanismo. Historia, costumbres y dialecto de los gitanos. Con un epítome de gramática gitana... y un diccionario caló-castellano. Madrid: Victoriano Suárez. (archive.org elgitanismohist00mayogoog)
sources.note: Epítome de gramática gitana, Preliminar p. 49: Caló 'tiene la misma escritura, alfabeto, ortografía y demás estructura gramatical que el castellano'; sect. 5 p. 51: inherited ('primitivos indostanes') masculine nouns end 'en consonante ó vocal acentuada', feminine in stressed í; sect. 12-13 pp. 64-65: inherited adjectives end in consonant or stressed á/é/ó/ú (fem. -í: chororí, languí), whereas adjectives taken from Castilian 'siguen las mismas reglas de su origen' with unstressed -e/-o. No prosody chapter; no general stress rule.
